translations.answer: H2O's sim-to-data filter uses a privileged motion imitator to reject retargeted motions that are difficult to execute under robot dynamics, and the paper's ablation supports improved deployment-policy success. However, RGB-only describes the human command input: robot linear velocity on hardware still comes from external motion capture, so the complete loop is not localization-free.
translations.applicability.assumptions.0: Human pose estimates, robot state, reference frames, and timestamps have been aligned.
translations.applicability.assumptions.1: The source of linear-velocity estimation is explicitly recorded in the deployment design.
translations.applicability.controllers.0: PPO whole-body imitation policy with joint PD targets.
translations.applicability.environments.0: Monocular human commands, simulation training, and H1 hardware teleoperation.
translations.confidence_rationale: Simulation ablations support the sim-to-data filter and state design. Confidence is capped because hardware evidence is demonstrative and robot linear velocity depends on external motion capture.
translations.evidence.0.locator: Figure 4, Tables III–IV, Figures 5–7, and Sections III–IV.
translations.evidence.0.note: Reports the two-stage data pipeline, success-rate ablations, deployable state, and external linear-velocity source.
translations.evidence.0.title: Learning Human-to-Humanoid Real-Time Whole-Body Teleoperation
translations.terms.0: Proportional-Derivative Control (比例-微分控制, PD Control)
translations.title: Why does H2O filter motions with a privileged policy, and does RGB alone close the robot loop?
